title: A packet dissector
description:
Build a small `tcpdump`: give it a pcap file and it prints one line per packet, decoding Ethernet, IPv4, TCP, UDP and DNS, and saying plainly when a packet is truncated or malformed instead of reading past its end.

```cpp
std::string dissect(const std::vector<std::uint8_t>& frame);
std::vector<std::string> dissectFile(const std::vector<std::uint8_t>& pcap);
```

**Ethernet.** A frame shorter than 14 bytes is `[truncated]`. One VLAN tag (`0x8100`) is allowed, as in practice 4.02. Then, by EtherType:

| EtherType | Line |
|---|---|
| `0x0806` | `ARP` |
| `0x86DD` | `IP6 next header N, length L`, from the IPv6 header's next header and payload length; `[truncated]` if the 40-byte header does not fit |
| `0x0800` | the IPv4 rules below |
| anything else | `ethertype 0x88cc, length 60`: four lower-case hex digits and the frame's size |

**IPv4.** If fewer than 20 bytes follow the Ethernet header, the line is `[truncated]`. If the version is not 4, the header length is under 20, or the total length is less than the header length, it is `[malformed]`. If the header is longer than the bytes available, `[truncated]`. Otherwise the IP data is the bytes after the header, up to the total length or the end of the captured frame, whichever comes first (a capture's snapshot length may have cut the packet short, and Ethernet padding is not data). **L**, the data length, is always `total length - header length`, whatever was captured. `A` and `B` below are the source and destination in dotted decimal, `a` and `b` the source and destination ports.

| Packet | Line |
|---|---|
| fragment offset not 0 | `IP A > B: fragment offset O, length L`, O in bytes |
| TCP (6) | `IP A.a > B.b: Flags [F], seq S, ack K, win W, length P` |
| UDP (17) | `IP A.a > B.b: UDP, length P`, or a DNS summary |
| ICMP (1) | `IP A > B: ICMP, length L` |
| anything else | `IP A > B: proto N, length L` |

A packet whose IP header checksum is wrong still decodes, and its line ends with ` [bad checksum]`.

**TCP.** If fewer than 20 bytes of TCP header were captured: `IP A > B: [truncated]`. If the TCP header length is under 20 or longer than L: `IP A > B: [malformed]`. If the header (options included) was not all captured: `IP A > B: [truncated]`. The flags are written as letters in the order `S` (SYN), `F` (FIN), `R` (RST), `P` (PSH), `U` (URG), then `.` for ACK, or `none` if there are none: so a SYN-ACK is `[S.]`. The `, ack K` part appears only when ACK is set. P is `L - TCP header length`. Only the headers need to have been captured, not the data.

**UDP.** If fewer than 8 bytes were captured: `IP A > B: [truncated]`. If the UDP length is under 8 or more than L: `IP A.a > B.b: [malformed]`. P is `UDP length - 8`. If either port is 53, try to read DNS from the UDP data (up to the UDP length or the end of what was captured): at least a 12-byte header, at least one question, and a question name made of plain labels (no compression pointers) followed by 4 bytes of type and class, all inside the data. The root name is written `.`. Then the line is `IP A.a > B.b: ` followed by:

- `DNS query NAME` if the QR bit is 0;
- `DNS response NAME, no such name` if the response code is 3;
- otherwise `DNS response NAME, 1 answer` or `DNS response NAME, N answers`.

If the DNS cannot be read, the line is the ordinary `UDP, length P`.

**dissectFile** reads a pcap file in either byte order, with microsecond or nanosecond timestamps (practice 4.01). If the header is bad or the link type is not 1 (Ethernet), it returns no lines. For each complete record it adds `T ` and the record's `dissect` line, where T is the time since the first packet as seconds with six decimals (`0.750100`; nanoseconds are cut to microseconds, and a time earlier than the first packet shows as `0.000000`). An incomplete record at the end is left out.
hints: Write the decoder top-down, one layer per block, and before each block ask: how many bytes do I need, and how many are really there? Keep two different "ends" for IP: the length the header claims (for reporting lengths) and the bytes actually captured (for reading).

Build each output line from a prefix that is decided as soon as the addresses are known (`IP A > B: `) and a prefix with ports once the transport header is read (`IP A.a > B.b: `). The truncated and malformed lines then fall out of the same structure.
requirements: Every line follows the formats above exactly.
Ethernet with or without a VLAN tag, ARP, IPv6 and unknown EtherTypes are recognised.
IPv4, TCP and UDP headers are decoded with their real lengths, ignoring padding and coping with packets cut short by the capture.
DNS queries and responses on port 53 are summarised, and unreadable DNS falls back to UDP.
Nothing is ever read past the end of the frame: short and inconsistent packets give `[truncated]` or `[malformed]`.
pcap files in both byte orders and both timestamp precisions are read, with relative times.
stretch: Read a pcap file from disk named on the command line, print the lines, and compare your output with `tcpdump -nn -r capture.pcap` or Wireshark's packet list on a capture of your own local traffic.
